content: There are still unresolved questions regarding the optimal strategies for implementing care for children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. A key concern is how to enhance testing and linkage to care for these populations, as well as how to improve access to pediatric-appropriate formulations of antiviral medications. To better understand the prevalence and burden of HCV in children and adolescents, age-stratified serosurveys assessing HCV antibody prevalence and viremia should be conducted. These surveys should include both high-risk groups, such as children born to HCV-infected mothers or those exposed through repeated transfusions or high-risk medical procedures, and the general population. The regional burden of disease, associated morbidity, and treatment needs should be carefully estimated. Furthermore, children and adolescents should be incorporated into routine national data collection systems and global reporting frameworks for the viral hepatitis care cascade, which includes diagnosis, treatment, and cure. Addressing these gaps will require additional efforts and the active engagement of all relevant stakeholders. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have been shown to be both effective and safe for treating children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection, regardless of age, treatment regimen, or duration. This conclusion is supported by evidence from three randomized controlled trials, 28 non-randomized controlled trials, and 18 observational studies. The available data provide sufficient evidence to support the treatment of chronic HCV infection in pediatric populations.
